title: Dedicated Workload Guardrails & Headroom Negotiation
creator: Aisha Nguyen
description: Background: Several customers running Dedicated capacity report either wasted idle reserved GPUs during low traffic or sudden request failures during short bursts because the existing reserved pool model is too binary: reserved vs. unreserved. We need a mechanism that lets tenants declare and negotiate temporary headroom and burst credits while preserving isolation guarantees and predictable SLOs for reserved commitments.

Goal: Introduce a Workload Guardrails layer and a Headroom Negotiation protocol that allow: (1) safe short-term burst above a tenant's reserved baseline using a credit ledger, (2) configurable soft headroom with preemption semantics, and (3) scheduler-enforced limits to avoid noisy-neighbor impacts. This should integrate with autoscaling so that autoscale decisions take headroom and recent burst debt into account.

Non-goals: This PRD does not change pricing, does not replace existing hard reservation semantics, and does not attempt to do predictive provisioning for all tenants. It also does not implement model-level QoS (that is future work).

User stories:
- As a platform operator, I want tenants to be able to request temporary headroom so that short traffic spikes succeed without permanently overprovisioning.
- As an SRE, I want the scheduler to limit total cross-tenant burst usage so one tenant cannot degrade others' latency SLOs.
- As an account owner, I want clear visibility into my burst credit usage, remaining headroom, and any preemptions that occurred during bursts.
success_metrics: Percent of burst requests served successfully when total cluster utilization < 90%: >= 95%
Reduction in customer-reported dedicated errors during short spikes (<= 2 min): 40% within 8 weeks of rollout
No regression in P95 latency for reserved tenants: < 5% relative increase
Console: Per-tenant burst credit and headroom dashboards available and refreshed under 30s
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler honors per-tenant soft headroom (%) and enforces global guardrail cap; violations are logged as events
Burst credit ledger persists metadata per-tenant and supports consume/repay semantics; credits can be queried via API and Console
Autoscaler incorporates headroom debt in its scaling decision: will not scale down below reserved baseline while tenant has outstanding burst debt
Graceful preemption: when global guardrail exceeded, lower-priority soft-headroom workloads are preempted with a configurable TTL to allow graceful completion (default 60s)
E2E tests proving eviction order and credit repayment semantics under synthetic load (scripts and results committed to repo)
Observability: Metrics (headroom_used, burst_credits_consumed, preemptions, guardrail_violations) emitted to console and included in per-tenant billing logs
Feature flag gated rollout with canary: initial enablement for 5 pilot tenants, then 25, then full rollout following acceptance tests
out_of_scope: Automated migration of tenants between Dedicated and Hosted based on burst behavior
high_level_design: Control plane: extend reservation metadata to include soft_headroom_pct and burst_credit_quota. A small ledger service tracks credit consumption and repayment events.

Scheduler: new guardrail plugin computes available global headroom budget and enforces per-tenant soft limits and preemption order based on priority epochs. Uses token-bucket style accounting for short bursts.
Autoscaler: consults ledger state before scaling decisions; avoids scale-down while tenant has outstanding debt or recent high burst frequency.
Console/UX: per-tenant page shows headroom, credit balance, recent preemptions and a timeline view. API endpoints added for credit introspection and admin adjustments.
rollout_plan: Feature flag development and unit/integration tests (2 weeks)
Internal dogfood: enable for Redwood internal tenants and infra team; collect telemetry (1 week)
Canary: enable for 5 pilot customers with SRE on-call and rollback runbook (2 weeks)
Gradual ramp: 25 customers, then 100, monitoring SLOs and error budgets (4 weeks)
Full GA: post-mortem and documentation published, update onboarding docs and console help (2 weeks)
open_questions: What should be the default soft_headroom_pct per pricing tier? (suggested: 20% for standard, 50% for enterprise)
Should burst credits be transferable between sub-accounts or projects?
How do we reflect burst debt in billing and invoices? (billing will be deferred to Q2 follow-up)
engineering_notes: We debated two approaches: (A) scheduler-only enforcement with approximate accounting, (B) lightweight ledger + scheduler. Chosen: ledger+scheduler to provide precise, auditable credits and easier Console integration.
Trade-offs: ledger increases control-plane write volume. Mitigation: batch writes and eventual-consistency windows for non-critical dashboards.

Implementation plan: add DB table reserve_ledger (sharded by tenant), scheduler plugin, autoscale hook, and Console APIs. Initial implementation will not support cross-region headroom aggregation (follow-up).
Spike results: synthetic load test showed token-bucket approach reduces noisy-neighbor preemptions by ~60% in a 50-tenant stress test (results in repo under /tests/headroom)
